messages.author: 7823eb471ad1d2ff
messages.subject: Creating Posterior Predictive Checks
parts:
Hi all,

I'm in the middle of a series of workshops on Bayesian data analysis
and Stan as part of Dublin R. I gave them a few years ago but decided
to run it again and switch the inference engine to Stan.

The materials for the workshop are all available in a bitbucket repo

https://bitbucket.org/kaybenleroll/dublin_r_workshops

The relevant stuff is in the wsbda201603 directory for anyone
interested. It's all a bit rough and ready.

Anyway, while I probably won't be covering it this month, I also want
to talk a little about posterior predictive checks - most likely in
the workshop next month.

I am building a hierarchical model for coins, coin tosses and mints as
described by Kruschke in DBDA.

Here is a snapshot of the data:

!> inputdata.dt
mint.id coin.id toss.count success
1: 1 1 888 437
2: 1 2 1034 524
3: 1 3 1033 490
4: 1 4 961 469
5: 1 5 931 428
---
2525: 5 2525 965 505
2526: 5 2526 943 498
2527: 5 2527 983 529
2528: 5 2528 1026 588
2529: 5 2529 1061 591


Thus, each datum contains an index for the mint and coin (each coin.id
is unique for the whole dataset). Each coin had an individual number
of trials, and the number of successes is also given.

I built a hierarchical model in the standard way, model the theta of
the coin as being drawn from a Beta distribution parameterised by mu
and K, with the mu and K being drawn from a higher Beta and a Gamma
distribution, each mint having its own prior.

I have kept the five mints separately for now, purely to keep things
simple, but figure now is a good time to introduce PPCs.

The idea is to use the data to assess the quality of the mints. Which
of the 5 mints produces the 'best' coins, best being defined as toss
probability being closest to 0.5 with the lowest variance.

Anyway, I was thinking about the good ways to set this up via the
generated quantities block. I can use each sample to generate a mu and
K for each mint and then generate coins and tosses after that. With
that I could perhaps generate what the overall probability of a
success is across all the coins generated, but also track the min and
max theta for each mint as a way to assess variance.

I know all of this is a little contrived, but it keeps things simple
and allows the attendees to focus on what is going on.

My big question is over how to capture the variance of the coin counts
and toss counts in the data. They are directly supplied rather than
being modelled, so is there a way to sample those counts in the
generated quantities block (like the sample() function in R) or should
I be thinking about this differently and just go with a fixed number
of coins and tosses for this?


Thanks for all your help. All the code I'm using is in the repo, but
please let me know if I am leaving out some details - I'm still a bit
hazy on the best way to use PPCs which is part of the motivation for
covering it in the workshop (I'm selfish that way).



--
Mick Cooney
mickc...@gmail.com

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Creating Posterior Predictive Checks
parts:
Thanks for the link and letting us know.

To save Andrew the trouble of responding, I'd use a more realistic
example than coins. He even wrote a paper on why coins are a bad
example:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/diceRev2.pdf

For pedagogical purposes, I'd only use one level of hierarchy to keep
things simple. That's what I did in my case study, along with
a range of posterior p-values, predictive checks, predictions, event
probability estimates, and calibration/sharpness tests for model comparison
(of complete pooling, no pooling, along with partial pooling with hierarchical
models:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html

You'll also see the log-odds parameterization with a comparison to
the beta (for which I used a different prior, following Gelman et al.s
Bayesian Data Analysis, chapter 5).

And yes, using the generated quantities for posterior predictive
checks is exactly what you want to do --- I give examples in the
case study and explain why you want to do it.

I can't tell if I keep pointing to this tutorial because I just wrote
it, or wrote it so I wouldn't have to keep repeating myself!

You don't need all this modeling to answer your "which is the best
mint" question --- to literally answer your question you could just pool
everything within the "mint" and evaluate log density with
binomial(N, 0.5) model. But really the question for mints isn't
flippability, but weight and size.

But that's probably not the question you really want to answer in
a real application, where either 0 or 1 is usually the target (infant
mortality vs. free throws, say).

- Bob

to fix much of it.

contribute should be a lot more practical once I finally get around to
properly writing it up.
